newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaraguan business seeks unity against Sandinistas.
newsitem.headline: Nicaraguan business seeks unity against Sandinistas.

text.p: Nicaragua's business community, alarmed by the prospect of left-wing Sandinistas winning Sunday's presidential election, on Tuesday urged Nicaraguans to unite to stop their return to power.
The largest business organisation, the Higher Council of Private Enterprise (COSEP), asked voters to back rightist candidate Arnoldo Aleman in the tightening race.
"The Sandinista Front is not capable of generating the confidence necessary for the private sector and foreign and national investment," COSEP said in a statement.

It said a Sandinista government was "totally unacceptable" given the "damage" they had caused from 1979 to 1990 when they governed with Soviet and Cuban backing, confiscating private property and introducing a planned Marxist economy.
CID-Gallup opinion polls show the Sandinistas have surged in the last few weeks of the election campaign to close a 17-point gap between them and Aleman to just 2.6 percent.

The Sandinistas, whose candidate is former President Daniel Ortega, have sought to moderate the party's radical image, selling themselves as a moderate, centre-left party that would respect private property and the free market.

Ortega has been trying to dispel fears of a return to the economic disorder of the 1980s and make a Sandinista victory more acceptable to the private sector and foreign governments. But he has moved carefully to avoid alienating labour unions and party activists who form his power base, analysts said.

On Monday, Ortega met with members of a militant taxi drivers union and promised them a series of concessions in exchange for their votes. The same day, he met with owners of foreign assembly plants in Nicaragua's free trade zone to assure them that their investments were secure.
His overtures to the plant owners put him at odds with the pro-Sandinista unions that charge that these assembly plants exploit the Nicaraguan workers.
"(The Sandinistas) have a double discourse: one for the left, to maintain their social base, and another for the dominant class with which they do business," said political analyst Rene Vargas.

Adding to leftist disaffection with the Sandinistas was the "pinata," under which party officials transferred a number of confiscated properties and businesses to their own names after they lost to President Violeta Chamorro in 1990.

"Sandinistas became bankers, industrialists, businessmen and owners of sugar refineries and large tracts of land," Vargas said. "The Sandinista leadership has ceased to be a left-wing option, but their social bases continue thinking they are."
